intro: The most common reason homeowners in Borthwickyard look into wet room installation is accessibility — either preparing a property for later life, accommodating a family member with mobility needs, or simply wanting a bathroom that feels genuinely spacious rather than cramped. A well-designed wet room removes the trip hazard of a shower tray, opens up the floor space, and adds real value to a home. In a small community like Borthwickyard, where properties tend to be well-maintained and owners take pride in their homes, this is typically a planned, considered investment rather than an emergency repair — and it deserves to be treated that way from the outset.
localContext: Borthwickyard sits in Midlothian and is made up largely of older stone-built properties and period cottages, with some modern estate homes in the mix. The character of these buildings matters enormously when it comes to wet room installation. Older stone construction often means solid floors rather than suspended timber, which is actually an advantage — solid floors are easier to waterproof and drain effectively. That said, stone walls can present challenges when chasing in pipework, and the thickness of older walls needs to be factored into the design. Period cottages in Borthwickyard may also have lower ceiling heights or irregular room shapes that require a more bespoke approach to layout and drainage positioning. The water in this part of Midlothian is moderately hard, which is worth bearing in mind when choosing fittings and shower heads — scale build-up is a real consideration, and specifying fittings that are easy to descale or installing a small inline filter will save frustration in the long run on any wet room project here.
serviceDetail: A wet room installation in Borthwickyard typically follows a clear sequence, and understanding each stage helps you know what to expect and how to plan around it. The process usually begins with a survey visit, where a qualified installer assesses the existing bathroom space, checks the floor construction, identifies where the waste pipe runs, and discusses your layout preferences. From there, a detailed design and specification is agreed, covering the drain position, gradient of the floor, wall tanking system, and choice of tiles or wall panels. Once work begins, the existing bathroom is stripped out completely. The floor is then prepared — either built up with a former to create the correct fall towards the drain, or cut into if a low-profile linear drain is being set into a solid floor. The critical stage is tanking: a waterproof membrane is applied to walls and floor, overlapping at all junctions and upstands, before any tiling begins. This is what makes a wet room genuinely waterproof rather than just a shower without a tray. Plumbing connections are made for the shower valve, any basin or WC, and the waste. Tiling or panelling is then completed, fixtures are fitted and sealed, and the space is thoroughly tested before handover. From start to finish, most wet room installations in Borthwickyard take between five and ten working days depending on complexity.
pricing: In Borthwickyard, a realistic budget for a wet room installation sits between £6,000 and £12,000 for a full professional job. A straightforward conversion of an existing bathroom with mid-range fittings and porcelain tiling typically comes in at the lower end of that range. Costs rise with larger rooms, premium fixtures such as thermostatic valves and frameless glass screens, underfloor heating, or any structural work needed to accommodate the drain. Older stone-built properties occasionally require additional work to level floors or re-route pipework, which can add to the overall cost. Always get a written, itemised quote so you know exactly what is and isn't included.
whyLocal: Choosing a tradesperson who knows Borthwickyard and the surrounding Midlothian area genuinely makes a difference on a job like this. Local installers are familiar with the construction quirks of older stone properties here — the kind of surprises that can appear once a bathroom is stripped out, from lime mortar substrates to unusual pipe runs. They also tend to have established relationships with local suppliers, which helps with lead times on tiles and sanitaryware. Perhaps most importantly, a local tradesperson has a reputation to protect in a small community, and that accountability counts for a great deal when you're investing up to £12,000 in your home.

faqs.q: Can a wet room be installed in an older stone-built cottage in Borthwickyard?
faqs.a: Yes, and it's done regularly in properties like these across Midlothian. Solid stone floors are actually well suited to wet room installation as they take tanking and drainage work well. The main considerations are ensuring the membrane is applied correctly over older substrates and that any pipework chased into stone walls is properly protected. An experienced installer will assess this during the initial survey.

faqs.q: How long does a wet room installation take in Borthwickyard?
faqs.a: Most installations take between five and ten working days. A straightforward conversion in a standard-sized bathroom is usually closer to five days, while larger rooms, complex drainage layouts, or properties requiring additional floor preparation — which is more common in older Borthwickyard cottages — may take closer to a full two weeks. Your installer should give you a realistic programme before work begins.

faqs.q: Will hard water affect my wet room fittings in Borthwickyard?
faqs.a: Borthwickyard has moderately hard water, so limescale will gradually build up on shower heads, glass screens, and chrome fittings if not maintained. Choosing fittings with an anti-scale nozzle design helps, and a simple weekly wipe-down with a descaling solution keeps things looking good. Some installers will also fit a small inline scale filter to the shower supply, which is worth considering on a premium installation.

faqs.q: What's the difference between a wet room and a walk-in shower, and which is better for my Borthwickyard home?
faqs.a: A walk-in shower uses a large tray with a low or flush edge, while a true wet room has the entire floor tanked and graded to drain, with no tray at all. Wet rooms offer more flexibility on size and layout, and are generally better for accessibility. In Borthwickyard's older properties with solid floors, both options are feasible, but a full wet room tends to be the more durable and visually seamless choice for a premium renovation.
